set1.q: A 47-year-old man with cardiac sarcoidosis has corticosteroid-refractory disease. He also has rheumatoid arthritis, and methotrexate he once took for it was stopped after it was implicated in lung injury. His team is weighing methotrexate, azathioprine, infliximab and continued corticosteroids. Which of these should be avoided?
opts: Cardiac involvement is an indication for oral corticosteroids, and refractory disease is the setting for adding an immunosuppressant to the plan. Tell: nothing in his history rules steroids out; the agent with a record of lung injury in him is methotrexate.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Methotrexate is one of the immunosuppressants used for corticosteroid-refractory sarcoidosis, but it has also been implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease, and in him it already was. Azathioprine or infliximab covers the same refractory indication without that history.

Infliximab is one of the immunosuppressants named for corticosteroid-intolerant or refractory sarcoidosis. Tell: nothing in his history counts against it, unlike the drug already implicated in his lung injury, so it remains a reasonable choice.

Azathioprine is named with methotrexate and infliximab for corticosteroid-refractory sarcoidosis. Tell: it carries no prior lung injury in his history, so it stays on the table while the drug implicated in that injury does not.

set1.q: A 58-year-old woman has 8 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and a persistent nonproductive cough, with bibasilar dry rales and small lung volumes on examination. Which combination of total lung capacity and ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity is expected?
opts: This is the reverse of the restrictive pattern, in which the ratio is normal or increased and total lung capacity is decreased. Tell: scarred, stiff lungs shrink, matching her small lung volumes on examination, rather than holding more air.

A low ratio does not fit the restrictive pattern, which keeps the ratio normal or increased. Tell: interstitial disease also lowers total lung capacity, so a normal capacity misses the defining change in her stiff, small lungs.

Normal values would miss the restriction that scarring produces once lung tissue stiffens. Tell: an examination can be normal early in the disease, but her small lung volumes and progressive dyspnea point to a reduced total lung capacity.
Low capacity, normal or high ratio

Correct. Interstitial lung disease stiffens the lung so it no longer expands, giving a restrictive pattern: total lung capacity and forced vital capacity fall while the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity stays normal or rises. Her small lung volumes on examination fit.

set1.q: A 50-year-old woman who has cut and polished stone for 22 years has silicosis. Her clinician reviews the complications linked to silicosis. Which connective tissue disease is among them?
opts: Correct. The complications listed for silicosis are an increased risk of tuberculosis, progressive massive fibrosis and scleroderma. Scleroderma is also one of the connective tissue diseases that produce interstitial lung disease, so new findings in her deserve that thought.

Rheumatoid arthritis is a connective tissue disease that can cause interstitial lung disease, and methotrexate used to treat it is a drug cause. Tell: it is not on the silicosis complication list, which names scleroderma as the connective tissue disease.

Systemic lupus erythematosus is among the connective tissue diseases with an inflammatory, fibrotic lung response, flagged by a high antinuclear antibody. Tell: the connective tissue disease linked to silicosis is scleroderma.

Sjögren's syndrome is a connective tissue cause of interstitial lung disease. Tell: silicosis complications are tuberculosis, progressive massive fibrosis and scleroderma, so Sjögren's syndrome is not among them for a stone worker.

How is this pattern classified?
opts: Her results meet the restrictive definition exactly: a normal or increased ratio with decreased total lung capacity and forced vital capacity. Tell: her ratio of 0.86 sits above the 0.70 normal limit given, so the low capacities stand alone as restriction, the pattern of interstitial lung disease.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A restrictive pattern is a normal or increased ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity with decreased total lung capacity and forced vital capacity. Her ratio of 0.86 is preserved while both capacities sit near 60% of predicted, the pattern interstitial lung disease produces.

Her ratio of 0.86 is above the normal limit given, so airflow is not the problem; her lung volumes are what have fallen. Tell: a preserved ratio with a low total lung capacity and forced vital capacity is the restrictive definition.

Her forced vital capacity and total lung capacity are both near 60% of predicted, well under the normal range of 80% or more. Tell: low volumes with a preserved ratio define restriction, which her crackles and dyspnea also suggest.

set1.q: A 66-year-old retired construction worker has asbestosis with exertional dyspnea and fine bibasilar crackles. He asks about a procedure to wash the asbestos fibers out of his lungs. Which treatment plan fits?
opts: The fibers cannot be removed by any means, and the fibrosis they cause is permanent scar tissue. Tell: corticosteroids appear in the plans for sarcoidosis and severe hypersensitivity pneumonitis, while asbestosis care is supportive.

Methotrexate is a corticosteroid alternative in sarcoidosis and is itself implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease. Tell: asbestosis treatment is supportive: oxygen therapy, physiotherapy, medications and vaccinations.

Correct. Treatment of asbestosis is supportive because asbestos fibers invade lung tissue and cannot be removed. Oxygen therapy, physiotherapy, medications and vaccinations make up that care, while the scarring itself comes from chronic inflammation and macrophage invasion forming fibrosis.
Lavage to wash out the fibers

Asbestos fibers cannot be removed from lung tissue once they invade it, which is why treatment is supportive. Tell: bronchoalveolar lavage is a diagnostic study, used in silicosis to show milky fluid, not a way to clear asbestos.

set1.q: A 41-year-old woman with sarcoidosis has a chest film showing diffuse reticular infiltrates throughout both lungs. Her previously enlarged hilar nodes are no longer seen, and there is no honeycombing or hilar retraction. Which radiographic stage is this?
opts: Stage I is bilateral hilar adenopathy alone with clear lungs. Tell: her hilar nodes are no longer enlarged and her lungs carry diffuse infiltrates, the opposite pattern to stage I in both features.
Stage II needs hilar adenopathy and parenchymal involvement together. Tell: her hilar nodes are no longer seen, leaving parenchymal disease alone, which is stage III rather than stage II.

Correct. Stage III is parenchymal involvement alone, seen as diffuse reticular infiltrates, with no hilar adenopathy. Her film has infiltrates without enlarged nodes and without the honeycombing, hilar retraction, bullae or cysts that would mark stage IV.

Stage IV is advanced fibrosis with honeycombing, hilar retraction, bullae, cysts or emphysema. Tell: her film has none of these, only diffuse reticular infiltrates, so she has not reached the fibrotic stage.

set1.q: A 57-year-old stone worker has had silicosis for 8 years. He asks which complication his lung disease puts him at increased risk of. Which is it?
opts: Hypercalcemia occurs in about 5% of patients with sarcoidosis and is an indication for corticosteroids there. Tell: silica dust causes silicosis, not sarcoidosis, and silicosis complications are tuberculosis, progressive massive fibrosis and scleroderma.

Goodpasture syndrome is glomerulonephritis with diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage in young adults, identified by basement membrane antibodies. Tell: it is not a silica complication; silicosis raises the risk of tuberculosis.

Correct. Silicosis carries an increased risk of tuberculosis, together with progressive massive fibrosis and scleroderma. That is why patients with silicosis should have a tuberculosis skin test and a current chest film, and why the risk deserves mention at follow-up.

Mesothelioma, a primarily pleural cancer, is nearly always caused by asbestos exposure, with a 10% lifetime risk in asbestos workers. Tell: his dust is silica from stone work, whose listed complications are tuberculosis, massive fibrosis and scleroderma.

set1.q: A 46-year-old man with severe pancreatitis develops profound dyspnea on hospital day 2. His chest film shows new bilateral opacities not explained by effusion, atelectasis or nodules, and an echocardiogram shows normal cardiac function. His arterial oxygen pressure is 62 mm Hg on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.40. How is his oxygenation impairment classified?
opts: The oxygenation criterion is a ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen under 300 mm Hg. Tell: 62 / 0.40 = 155, well under 300, so he meets the criterion and the question becomes which class.
Mild covers ratios of 200-300 mm Hg. Tell: his ratio, 62 / 0.40 = 155, is below 200, one class worse than mild; reading 62 against 300 without dividing by 0.40 is what makes mild look right.

Correct. Divide arterial oxygen pressure by fraction of inspired oxygen: 62 / 0.40 = 155 mm Hg. That is under the 300 threshold and falls between 100 and 200, the moderate class. Severe pancreatitis is a systemic trigger, and his new opacities and normal heart complete the criteria.

Severe is a ratio under 100 mm Hg, the class with the most impaired oxygenation. Tell: 62 / 0.40 = 155 sits above 100, so he has not reached the severe class; an arterial oxygen pressure of 62 alone is not the ratio.

set1.q: A 74-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis quit smoking at diagnosis. She asks whether any medicine has been shown to help her live longer. Which response is accurate?
opts: Fibrosis is permanent scar tissue, and corticosteroids may be used in some idiopathic pneumonia subtypes: cryptogenic organizing, lymphoid interstitial and nonspecific interstitial pneumonia. Tell: in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis nothing, steroids included, has improved survival compared with no treatment.

Methotrexate is used for corticosteroid-intolerant sarcoidosis and is itself implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease. Tell: in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis nothing has improved survival compared with no treatment, and this drug can injure the lung itself.

A surgical lung biopsy is a diagnostic test, and patients over 65 who meet the four criteria do not need one. Tell: biopsy defines the disease rather than removing it, and fibrosis is permanent scar tissue spread across the lungs.

Correct. Management of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is controversial: nothing has been shown to improve survival or quality of life compared with no treatment. Accurate diagnosis helps identify patients who may benefit from available therapies, and her smoking cessation remains critical to prolonging life.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man is found to have interstitial lung disease on computed tomography after months of exertional dyspnea and dry cough. No cause has been identified yet. Which part of his history looks for the most common group of known causes?
opts: Correct. The most common interstitial lung diseases of known etiology come from occupational or environmental exposures: inorganic dusts, organic dusts, and fumes or gases. Asking about his work and surroundings looks for agents such as asbestos fibers, silica dust, or moldy hay and bird excreta.

Interstitial lung disease is not caused by an infectious etiology, so a history of chest infections does not search for its known causes. Tell: the most common known causes are inhaled at work or in the environment, as inorganic dusts, organic dusts, fumes and gases.

Radiation, methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin and chemotherapeutics are treatment-related known causes, but they are not the group named as the most common. Tell: the most common interstitial lung diseases of known etiology come from occupational or environmental exposures.
Age and sex at symptom onset

Age and sex help diagnose the subtype of idiopathic interstitial pneumonia, together with prodrome, imaging and histology, but they do not name a cause. Tell: a known cause is an agent he was exposed to, most often at work or in the environment.

set1.q: A 59-year-old former shipyard worker with asbestosis smokes a pack of cigarettes a day. He asks what his cigarettes add to his asbestos exposure. Which risk do they markedly increase?
opts: Correct. In asbestos workers, cigarette smoking increases the prevalence of radiographic pleural and parenchymal changes and markedly increases the incidence of lung carcinoma. Asbestosis already carries an increased risk of lung cancer, especially in a smoker.

An increased risk of tuberculosis is a complication of silicosis, which is why those patients need a tuberculosis skin test and a current chest film. Tell: the risk that smoking markedly raises in asbestos workers is lung carcinoma.

Hypercalcemia is a laboratory finding in about 5% of patients with sarcoidosis and an indication for corticosteroids there. Tell: it belongs to a granulomatous disease of unknown cause, while his risk comes from asbestos plus cigarettes.

Progressive massive fibrosis is the complicated form of coal workers' pneumoconiosis and a complication of silicosis, a conglomeration of the upper lungs. Tell: his exposure is asbestos, where smoking drives up lung carcinoma.

set1.q: A 66-year-old retired coal miner with coal workers' pneumoconiosis and chronic dyspnea asks what can be done for his lungs. He already uses home oxygen and stopped smoking years ago. Which measure belongs in his care?
opts: Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome on the ventilator. Tell: he has chronic dust-related fibrosis managed at home, not an acute ventilated syndrome, so positioning has no role here.

Correct. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis has no effective curative treatment, so care is supportive: oxygen, pneumococcal and influenza vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation, with lung transplant for severe cases. With oxygen in place and smoking stopped, vaccination is the supportive measure still to add.

No effective curative treatment is available for coal workers' pneumoconiosis; care is supportive. Tell: an offer of cure contradicts the disease's management, which centers on oxygen, vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation.

Avoiding the responsible organic agent treats hypersensitivity pneumonitis, such as farmer's lung or bird fancier's lung. Tell: his disease comes from coal dust, which he no longer inhales since retiring, and moldy hay and birds play no part.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man is recovering after 3 weeks in the intensive care unit for acute respiratory distress syndrome. He has muscle wasting, weakness and persistent fatigue. Which referral addresses these problems?
opts: Yearly ophthalmologic evaluation is sarcoidosis follow-up for ocular inflammation. Tell: his needs after intensive care are muscle strength and fatigue, which rehabilitation addresses, not eye monitoring.

Correct. Long-term recovery after acute respiratory distress syndrome includes treating physical sequelae: post-intensive care muscle wasting, weakness and persistent fatigue. Rehabilitation addresses them while his lung function continues to improve over 6 to 12 months.

Lung transplant is listed for severe coal workers' pneumoconiosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tell: his problems are muscle wasting and weakness after intensive care, while his lungs are still recovering on their usual timeline.

Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is a salvage option for severe, refractory disease during the acute illness. Tell: he is in recovery, and his problems are physical sequelae of intensive care, not refractory hypoxemia.

opts: Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome on mechanical ventilation. Tell: his disease is a hypersensitivity reaction to hay, where severe cases call for corticosteroids.

High-frequency oscillatory ventilation provides no proven benefit even in acute respiratory distress syndrome, where it is listed to avoid. Tell: his severe hypersensitivity pneumonitis calls for corticosteroids, not a ventilator mode.
Return to work with a mask

Continued exposure may lead to a worsened disease state, so going back to the hay keeps the cause in play. Tell: the first step is to identify and avoid the agent, and severe disease then adds corticosteroids.

Correct. After the agent is identified and avoided, corticosteroids may be helpful in severe cases of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, with other immunosuppressants and supportive care such as oxygen. His persistent hypoxia, cyanosis, tachypnea and tachycardia despite avoidance mark severe disease.

opts: Corticosteroids are reserved for a few rare idiopathic interstitial pneumonia subtypes, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is not among them. Tell: no therapy has improved survival in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, while stopping his cigarettes is critical to prolonging life.

Identifying and avoiding the responsible agent is the first treatment of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which follows inhaled organic dust. Tell: his disease is idiopathic, with no antigen to avoid, and his modifiable cause is cigarettes.

Methotrexate is used for sarcoidosis that is corticosteroid-intolerant or refractory, and it is itself implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease. Tell: his disease is not sarcoidosis, and quitting cigarettes is the step that prolongs life.

Correct. Smoking is the cause in the majority of cases, 67 to 75% of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis have a smoking history, and cessation is critical to prolong life. Management is otherwise controversial, because nothing has improved survival or quality of life compared with no treatment.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man did demolition work around asbestos insulation for 20 years. He now has a pleural effusion, and mesothelioma is suspected. Which test can establish the diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Mesothelioma, a primarily pleural cancer nearly always caused by asbestos exposure, frequently produces pleural effusions, and it can be diagnosed from pleural fluid cytology. His long asbestos exposure and new effusion make the fluid the sample to examine.

Bronchoalveolar lavage returning thick, milky fluid with foamy macrophages is a silicosis finding. Tell: mesothelioma is a cancer of the pleural lining, so the sample comes from his pleural fluid, not from the airways.

A tuberculosis skin test with a current chest film is advised in silicosis because of its tuberculosis risk. Tell: his exposure is asbestos, and his effusion raises a pleural cancer, which is diagnosed from pleural fluid cytology.

A high antinuclear antibody points to a collagen vascular disease as a cause of interstitial lung disease. Tell: an asbestos worker with a pleural effusion and suspected mesothelioma needs the effusion itself examined by cytology.

She now has progressive exertional dyspnea, a dry cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles and a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing. She asks whether her arthritis medicine could be involved. Which response is accurate?
opts: No, drug injury needs cancer chemotherapy

The drug causes reach beyond chemotherapy: the treatment-related group includes methotrexate, amiodarone and nitrofurantoin as well as chemotherapeutics. Tell: methotrexate is named in that group in its own right, whatever disease it is given for.
Yes, methotrexate deposits dust in the lungs

Dust deposition in the alveoli is how silica and coal cause pneumoconiosis, through macrophage invasion and fibrosis. Tell: methotrexate is a drug cause in the treatment-related group, not an inhaled dust, so the mechanism offered is wrong.
Yes, methotrexate can cause this disease

Correct. Methotrexate is used for many autoimmune diseases, including lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, and it has also been implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease. Rheumatoid arthritis is itself a connective tissue cause, so her disease and her treatment both belong in the differential.

Methotrexate, a common treatment for rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, is in the treatment-related group of interstitial lung disease causes. Tell: her years of methotrexate are a recognized cause of exactly this disease, so the medicine cannot be dismissed.

opts: Early disease can have a normal exam

Correct. Early in interstitial lung disease the physical examination may be normal; small lung volumes, bibasilar dry rales or inspiratory crackles and distal clubbing appear as the disease develops. Her scan already shows the disease, so a normal examination does not mean healthy lungs.
A normal exam rules out lung disease

A normal examination does not exclude interstitial disease, because the examination may be normal early in its course. Tell: her computed tomography already shows the disease, which outweighs a normal examination at this early stage.

Crackles are a physical finding that may still be absent early, while imaging can already show change. Tell: her scan shows disease and her chest sounds normal, the reverse of crackles coming first, which is the point of her case.
Clubbing is the first sign to appear

Clubbing is listed among examination findings that come with disease progression, as in asbestosis, where crackles and clubbing appear as the disease advances. Tell: early disease may have no examination findings at all, which is her situation.

Within 24 hours he has refractory hypoxemia and new bilateral opacities on chest film with a normal heart size, and an echocardiogram shows normal cardiac function. On the ventilator his arterial oxygen pressure is 54 mm Hg on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.60. How is his oxygenation impairment classified?
opts: The criterion is met whenever the ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen is under 300 mm Hg. Tell: 54 / 0.60 = 90, far below 300, so he clearly meets the oxygenation criterion and sits in the worst class.

Mild is a ratio of 200-300 mm Hg, the least impaired class that still meets the criterion. Tell: his ratio of 54 / 0.60 = 90 is less than half the bottom of the mild range, two classes worse than mild.
Moderate covers 100-200 mm Hg. Tell: 54 / 0.60 = 90 falls just under 100, which crosses into the severe class; rounding up toward 100 is the mistake that makes moderate look right.

Correct. Divide arterial oxygen pressure by fraction of inspired oxygen: 54 / 0.60 = 90 mm Hg. A ratio under 100 is the severe class. Near-drowning is a direct pulmonary insult, and new bilateral opacities within a day with a normal heart complete the criteria.

set1.q: A 54-year-old man with newly diagnosed interstitial lung disease asks how the inflammation in his lungs turns into scar tissue. Which sequence is accurate?
opts: Correct. Macrophages, lymphocytes, monocytes and neutrophils accumulate in the alveolar walls, producing alveolitis. Alveolitis leads to fibroblast production, and the collagen the fibroblasts produce causes the fibrosis: permanent scar tissue that stiffens the lung and impairs gas exchange.

This runs the chain backward: collagen is the end product that forms the scar, not the starting event. Tell: the sequence begins with inflammatory cells gathering in the alveolar walls, which is alveolitis, and ends with collagen laid down as fibrosis.

Fibroblasts do not start the process; they are produced in response to alveolitis. Tell: inflammatory cells in the alveolar walls create the alveolitis first, the fibroblasts follow, and their collagen comes last as permanent scar.

Collagen is made by the fibroblasts, so it cannot appear before them. Tell: alveolitis leads to fibroblast production, and those fibroblasts then produce the collagen that causes fibrosis, the stiff scar that impairs gas exchange.

opts: Repeat chest film in a year

Yearly chest films belong to sarcoidosis follow-up once the diagnosis is made. Tell: waiting a year leaves possible lymphoma undiagnosed; the findings that raise lymphoma make biopsy essential now rather than later.

Correct. Biopsy is essential whenever clinical and radiographic findings suggest an alternative diagnosis such as lymphoma. Transbronchial lung or fine-needle node biopsy also confirms sarcoidosis itself by showing noncaseating granulomas, so tissue settles the question either way.

Corticosteroids treat sarcoidosis once it is confirmed and an indication such as hypercalcemia or uveitis is present. Tell: with lymphoma still possible, the diagnosis is unsettled, and biopsy is essential before treatment begins.

Angiotensin-converting enzyme is elevated in only 40-80% of patients with sarcoidosis, so it can support but not settle the diagnosis. Tell: when findings suggest an alternative diagnosis such as lymphoma, biopsy is the step named as essential.

set1.q: A 72-year-old woman develops profound dyspnea and new bilateral opacities 36 hours after multiple blood transfusions for a gastrointestinal bleed. She has a history of heart failure. What is the next step before acute respiratory distress syndrome can be diagnosed?
opts: Correct. The diagnosis requires respiratory failure not fully explained by heart failure or fluid overload, and echocardiographic assessment of cardiac function excludes hydrostatic cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Multiple transfusions are a recognized trigger, but her heart failure history makes that exclusion essential.

Routine pulmonary artery catheters offer no clinical benefit in acute respiratory distress syndrome and are avoided. Tell: cardiac function is assessed with echocardiography, which answers the heart failure question without a catheter.

Pulmonary function testing shows the restrictive pattern of chronic interstitial lung disease. Tell: in an acutely hypoxemic patient after transfusion, the open question is cardiac function, which echocardiography answers.
Serum antibodies to an inhaled agent

Serum antibodies to an inhaled agent give the definitive diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tell: her trigger is transfusion, not an organic dust, and the competing diagnosis to exclude is cardiogenic edema.

She has tachypnea, intercostal retractions and crackles, and her hypoxemia does not improve with supplemental oxygen. Her chest film shows new bilateral opacities with a normal heart size, and an echocardiogram shows normal cardiac function. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows inhaled organic dust, with symptoms hours after exposure and little change on early imaging. Tell: her trigger is sepsis, and her film shows new bilateral opacities with refractory hypoxemia.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis develops insidiously over years, with clubbing and pleural-based honeycombing. Tell: her opacities appeared within 30 hours of sepsis, an acute course after a known insult, not a slow fibrosis.

Correct. About one-third of cases present with sepsis, and profound dyspnea develops 12-48 hours after the insult. New bilateral opacities within 7 days, hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen and a normal heart on film and echocardiogram fit this non-cardiogenic syndrome.

Cardiogenic pulmonary edema displays cardiomegaly, vascular engorgement and batwing perihilar opacities, and echocardiography is used to exclude it. Tell: her heart size and cardiac function are both normal, so the edema is not cardiogenic.

An echocardiogram shows normal cardiac function. Her arterial oxygen pressure is 75 mm Hg on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.30. How is her oxygenation impairment classified?
opts: The criterion requires a ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen under 300 mm Hg. Tell: 75 / 0.30 = 250, under 300, so she meets the criterion, in its mildest class.

Correct. Divide arterial oxygen pressure by fraction of inspired oxygen: 75 / 0.30 = 250 mm Hg, which is under the 300 threshold and inside the 200-300 range of the mild class. Lung contusion is a direct pulmonary insult, and new bilateral opacities within 7 days with normal cardiac function complete the criteria.
Moderate is 100-200 mm Hg. Tell: her ratio, 75 / 0.30 = 250, sits above 200, in the mild band; an arterial oxygen pressure of 75 on its own says nothing until it is divided by the inspired fraction.
Severe is a ratio under 100 mm Hg. Tell: 75 / 0.30 = 250 is far above that; a low arterial oxygen pressure alone does not make the class severe once the inspired fraction is divided in.

opts: Hilar adenopathy alone carries the best prognosis, which can tempt watchful waiting. Tell: her calcium of 11.9 mg/dL is hypercalcemia, a listed indication for oral corticosteroids, so observation leaves an indication untreated.
ruled out by a stated finding

Bronchodilators are a supportive treatment in hypersensitivity pneumonitis, alongside oxygen and pain medication. Tell: her hypercalcemia is a steroid indication in sarcoidosis, and bronchodilators are not among the sarcoidosis treatments.

Correct. Her calcium of 11.9 mg/dL is above the 8.5-10.5 range, and hypercalcemia is one of the indications for oral corticosteroids in sarcoidosis. About 90% of cases respond to corticosteroids, so they come first even when the chest film shows hilar adenopathy alone.

Methotrexate, with azathioprine and infliximab, is used when patients are intolerant of corticosteroids or have corticosteroid-refractory disease. Tell: she has not yet had corticosteroids, so an immunosuppressant is the later step, not the first.

set1.q: A 56-year-old coal miner has severe complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis with worsening dyspnea despite oxygen, vaccinations, pulmonary rehabilitation and smoking cessation. Which referral may be indicated?
opts: Correct. Management of coal workers' pneumoconiosis is supportive, with oxygen, vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation, and in severe cases lung transplant may be indicated. He has severe disease that is worsening despite every supportive measure on the list.

No effective curative treatment is available, and the listed management is supportive care with lung transplant for severe cases. Tell: removing the dust is not among the options described; replacing the lung is the step named for severe disease.

Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is a salvage option reserved for severe, refractory acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: his disease is chronic dust-related fibrosis, for which the severe-case option is lung transplant, not acute salvage support.

Yearly ophthalmologic evaluation is part of sarcoidosis follow-up, to find and manage ocular inflammation. Tell: coal workers' pneumoconiosis has no eye monitoring step, and his severe, worsening lung disease points to transplant evaluation.

set1.q: A 41-year-old cheese maker has recurrent fever, chills, cough and dyspnea hours after handling moldy cheese at work. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is diagnosed, and her symptoms are mild. What is the first step in treatment?
opts: Corticosteroids may be helpful in severe cases of hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tell: her disease is mild, and without removing the moldy cheese exposure the disease can keep worsening, so avoidance comes first.

Lung transplant sits at the far end of the hypersensitivity pneumonitis treatment list. Tell: her disease is mild and may be reversible if the agent is removed early, so she is nowhere near transplant.

Bronchodilators are supportive treatment, with oxygen and pain medication. Tell: supportive care alone leaves her exposed to the moldy cheese, and continued exposure may lead to a worsened disease state.

Correct. Treatment of hypersensitivity pneumonitis starts by identifying the agent responsible and avoiding it. Prompt diagnosis is key to removing the patient from the irritating environment: symptoms can be reversible if caught early, while continued exposure may worsen the disease.

set1.q: A 69-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history has 18 months of insidious dry cough, exertional dyspnea and fatigue. He has clubbing, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, tachypnea and reduced chest expansion. Computed tomography shows diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing. He has no occupational exposures, medicines or connective tissue disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Asbestosis follows years of asbestos exposure in insulation, demolition, shipyard or construction work, with pleural plaques as its most common film finding. Tell: he has no occupational exposure, so there is no asbestos source.
ruled out by a stated finding

Sarcoidosis brings noncaseating granulomas, bilateral hilar adenopathy and onset in the third and fourth decades. Tell: a 69-year-old smoker with pleural-based honeycombing and no adenopathy described fits idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows inhaled organic dust, such as moldy hay or bird excreta, with malaise, chills and fever hours after exposure. Tell: he has no exposure, and his disease came on insidiously over 18 months.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Insidious dry cough, exertional dyspnea, fatigue, clubbing, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, tachypnea and reduced chest expansion are the picture of idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia, and pleural-based honeycombing with no associated cause is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Most patients have a smoking history.

opts: Yes, by acting as an inhaled dust

Inhaled inorganic dusts, organic dusts and fumes make up the occupational and environmental group, as in silicosis or farmer's lung. Tell: radiation belongs to the treatment-related group, not to the inhaled exposures, so the mechanism offered is wrong.
Yes, radiation is a recognized cause

Correct. Radiation is one of the treatment-related causes of interstitial lung disease of known cause, listed with methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin and chemotherapeutics. It is also named among the causes that provoke an inflammatory and fibrotic lung response, so her chest radiation is a credible cause.
No, radiation affects the skin alone

Radiation reaches more than the skin: it is a treatment-related cause of interstitial lung disease and is listed among causes with an inflammatory and fibrotic lung response. Tell: her past chest radiation is a recognized cause of exactly this lung disease.
No, cancer treatment spares the lungs

Cancer treatment does not spare the lungs: both radiation and chemotherapeutics are treatment-related causes of interstitial lung disease. Tell: her treatment history is part of the cause search, and her chest radiation stands out in it.

Over several months he has developed progressive exertional dyspnea, a dry cough and bibasilar inspiratory crackles, and pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern. He has no occupational exposures. How is his interstitial lung disease classified?
opts: The occupational group of known cause includes asbestosis and silicosis, which need years of work exposure to asbestos fibers or silica dust. Tell: he has no occupational exposure; the known cause in his history is a medicine he takes.
ruled out by a stated finding

Granulomatous lung disease covers sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis, where organized granulomas form in response to inflammation. Tell: nothing in his history points to granulomas or an inhaled organic antigen; his medicine list points to a drug cause.

Correct. Amiodarone sits with radiation, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin and chemotherapeutics in the treatment-related group of interstitial lung disease of known cause. His exertional dyspnea, dry cough, crackles and restrictive pattern fit interstitial disease, and his years of amiodarone supply the cause.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the diagnosis only when no associated cause is evident, even in a patient over 65 with crackles and restriction. Tell: amiodarone is an associated cause in his history, so his disease cannot be called idiopathic.

opts: Bilateral hilar adenopathy alone is stage I sarcoidosis, with no parenchymal involvement at all. Tell: her disease is parenchymal fibrosis with lower-field markings, the reverse of an adenopathy-only film.
Interstitial markings in the lower lung fields

Correct. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis the radiograph shows increased interstitial markings in the lower lung fields, with progressive fibrosis over several areas, matching her bibasilar crackles. Upper lung field nodules belong to coal and silica dust instead.
Nodular opacities in the upper lung fields

Nodular opacities in the upper lung fields, coal macules 2-5 mm across, mark coal workers' pneumoconiosis. Tell: her disease is idiopathic with markings at the bases, not dust nodules at the top of the lungs.
Eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes

Eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes is a silicosis finding, from free crystalline silica dust. Tell: that is a lymph node sign of silica exposure, while her disease shows interstitial markings in the lower lung fields.

opts: Nodular opacities are nodules, and a reticulonodular pattern overlaps reticular shadows with nodules, as in sarcoidosis. Tell: her film shows curvilinear reticular change, honeycombing, with no nodules described.
Progression from early to late disease

Correct. Among reticular opacities, fine ground-glass change is an early finding and medium reticular change, honeycombing, is a late finding. Moving from ground glass to honeycombing over 5 years marks progression, consistent with fibrosis, which damages the alveoli permanently.
Healing from active to inactive disease

Honeycombing is not a healed state: it is the late reticular finding of interstitial disease, and fibrosis is permanent scar tissue. Tell: her films ran from the early pattern, ground glass, to the late one, which is progression, not recovery.

Coarse reticular opacities are cystic spaces, a separate descriptor from honeycombing. Tell: her film is reported as medium reticular change with honeycombing, the named late finding, not coarse cystic spaces.

opts: An acute presentation develops over days to weeks and occurs with allergy. Tell: his illness is not one event but four separate bouts over a year that clear completely in between, a recurring rather than a single acute course.

A subacute presentation runs over weeks to months and may occur in any interstitial lung disease. Tell: his symptoms resolve completely between bouts instead of building steadily over weeks to months, which is the episodic pattern.

A chronic presentation runs over months to years and is how most interstitial lung diseases present, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and pneumoconiosis. Tell: chronic disease keeps building, while his bouts clear completely in between.

Correct. Interstitial lung disease can present acutely over days to weeks, subacutely over weeks to months, chronically over months to years, or episodically. The episodic pattern of recurrent bouts is less common and can be seen with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which makes his exposures worth reviewing.

She has no occupational, bird or mold exposures. What is the most likely cause of her interstitial lung disease?
opts: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the diagnosis when no associated cause is evident, even in a patient over 65 with crackles and a restrictive pattern. Tell: her long-term nitrofurantoin is an associated cause, so her disease cannot be called idiopathic.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows inhaled organic dust, such as moldy hay, bird excreta or moldy products, with malaise, chills and fever hours after exposure. Tell: she has no bird or mold exposure; her history points to a medicine instead.
ruled out by a stated finding

Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disease of unknown cause with onset in the third and fourth decades, hilar adenopathy and skin or eye findings. Tell: she is 66 with a known drug exposure and none of those multi-organ findings.

Correct. Nitrofurantoin is one of the treatment-related causes of interstitial lung disease, beside radiation, methotrexate, amiodarone and chemotherapeutics, and it is also named among drugs that cause pulmonary toxicity. Years of use followed by exertional dyspnea, dry cough, crackles and restriction fit a drug cause.

opts: Correct. Occupational and environmental exposures are grouped as inorganic dusts, organic dusts and fumes or gases. Stone work releases free crystalline silica, and pneumoconiosis is caused by inhaled coal dust or various inorganic or silicate dusts, so his exposure is an inorganic dust.

Organic dusts are the hypersensitivity pneumonitis sources: moldy hay, bird excreta and feathers, moldy sugarcane pulp and other moldy products. Tell: crystalline silica from stone is a silicate dust, which places his exposure in the inorganic group.

Fumes and gases form the third exposure category, beside inorganic and organic dusts. Tell: cutting and polishing stone raises a dust of free crystalline silica, a silicate dust that causes pneumoconiosis, not a fume or gas.

Her arterial oxygen pressure is 51 mm Hg on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.90. Which option is reserved for her situation?
opts: High-frequency oscillatory ventilation provides no proven benefit in acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: switching to an oscillatory mode is listed to avoid, while salvage for refractory severe disease is extracorporeal support.

Inotrope-driven excessive oxygen delivery causes potential harm, which is why supranormal targets are avoided. Tell: her refractory severe hypoxemia, with a ratio near 57, is a salvage problem, not a target for higher delivery.

A conservative fluid protocol is preferred, because restrictive fluids increase ventilator-free days. Tell: liberal fluids run against that strategy, and refractory severe disease at a ratio near 57 calls for extracorporeal support.

Correct. Her ratio is 51 / 0.90, about 57 mm Hg, well under 100, so she has severe acute respiratory distress syndrome that is refractory to ventilation strategy and prone positioning. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is the salvage option reserved for severe, refractory cases.

opts: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is confirmed by serum antibodies to an inhaled organic agent after an exposure. Tell: no exposure is described, and his positive cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody pairs with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Correct. A positive cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, one of the granulomatous vasculitides that produce interstitial lung disease with a granulomatous response. His biopsy showing granulomas with vasculitis fits that pairing.

Sarcoidosis is granulomatous too, with noncaseating granulomas, but its laboratory clues are an increased sedimentation rate, eosinophilia, hypercalcemia and an elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme. Tell: the positive cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody pairs with polyangiitis.

Goodpasture syndrome is identified by antiglomerular and antipulmonary alveolar basement membrane antibodies, with glomerulonephritis and diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage. Tell: his biopsy shows granulomas with vasculitis, and his positive test is the cytoplasmic antibody.

opts: Stage I is bilateral hilar adenopathy alone, the stage with the best prognosis. Tell: honeycombing and hilar retraction are signs of fibrosis, which stage I lacks entirely, so his film is far beyond stage I.
Stage II is hilar adenopathy with parenchymal involvement. Tell: his hila are retracted by scarring rather than enlarged, and honeycombing marks advanced fibrosis, not the infiltrates of stage II.

Stage III is parenchymal involvement alone, seen as diffuse reticular infiltrates. Tell: honeycombing, hilar retraction and bullae go beyond infiltrates to advanced fibrosis, the defining feature of stage IV.

Correct. Stage IV is advanced fibrosis with evidence of honeycombing, hilar retraction, bullae, cysts and emphysema, which his film shows. About 20% of patients with lung involvement experience irreversible lung impairment from progressive fibrosis, bronchiectasis and cavitation.

opts: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis brings an insidious dry cough with clubbing, inspiratory crackles and pleural-based honeycombing, and its no-biopsy rule applies over 65. Tell: skin sores and liver, spleen and node enlargement point to a multi-organ granulomatous disease.

Correct. Lupus pernio, skin sores on the face, is the skin involvement of sarcoidosis, and a dry cough, insidious dyspnea, nontender lymphadenopathy and liver and spleen enlargement complete its multi-organ picture. Sarcoidosis also occurs more often in Black patients and in women.

Despite the shared word, lupus pernio is a sarcoidosis skin finding; systemic lupus erythematosus is a connective tissue cause of interstitial disease flagged by a high antinuclear antibody. Tell: facial sores with liver, spleen and node enlargement point to granulomas.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows organic dust exposure, with malaise, chills, fever and cough hours afterward. Tell: no exposure is described, and skin sores with liver, spleen and lymph node enlargement are multi-organ findings that dust does not explain.

Pulmonary function testing shows reduced vital capacity and total lung capacity, and his chest film shows pleural plaques with linear streaking at the bases. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows inhaled organic dust, with malaise, chills, fever and cough hours after exposure. Tell: insulation work is an inorganic fiber exposure, and pleural plaques with basal streaking point to asbestos.

Correct. Insulation and shipyard work are asbestos exposures, and patients usually seek attention about 15 years after exposure. Exertional dyspnea with rare cough, fine bibasilar crackles, clubbing, reduced vital capacity and total lung capacity, and pleural plaques, the most common film finding, fit asbestosis.

Silicosis follows silica dust from mining, sandblasting, quarry or stone work and favors the upper lobes, with eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes. Tell: his exposure was insulation in shipyards, and his changes sit at the bases with pleural plaques.

Coal workers' pneumoconiosis follows coal dust and shows nodular opacities, coal macules 2-5 mm across, in the upper lung fields. Tell: he never mined coal, and his film shows basal streaking with pleural plaques instead.

His arterial oxygen pressure is 80 mm Hg on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.50, and an echocardiogram has excluded cardiogenic edema. Which intervention decreases mortality at his severity?
opts: Routine pulmonary artery catheters offer no clinical benefit, and echocardiography has already assessed his heart. Tell: monitoring with a catheter does not lower mortality; early prone positioning does at his moderate severity.

Transfusion is given at a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL, and higher hemoglobin targets do not improve patient outcomes. Tell: raising hemoglobin is not the mortality-lowering step at a ratio of 160; prone positioning is.

Correct. His ratio is 80 / 0.50 = 160 mm Hg, moderate acute respiratory distress syndrome. Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe cases, so he qualifies, alongside the low tidal volume ventilation he is already receiving.

High-frequency oscillatory ventilation provides no proven benefit and is listed among approaches to avoid. Tell: at a ratio of 80 / 0.50 = 160, the strategy that lowers mortality is prone positioning, not an oscillatory mode.

set2.q: A 76-year-old man has had interstitial lung disease for 9 years, and his dyspnea now occurs at rest. An echocardiogram shows right heart failure. What does the right heart failure indicate about his lung disease?
opts: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema displays cardiomegaly, vascular engorgement and batwing perihilar opacities, a hydrostatic problem of the heart rather than scarred lung. Tell: his right heart failure follows 9 years of lung disease, the pattern of advanced interstitial disease.
It has entered an acute phase

An acute presentation develops over days to weeks, while most interstitial lung diseases present chronically over months to years. Tell: a 9-year course ending in right heart failure is chronic, advanced disease, not a new acute phase.
It is at an advanced stage

Correct. Right heart failure appears with advanced interstitial lung disease, and dyspnea that has spread from exertion to rest also marks progression. Early in the disease the examination may be normal, so these findings place him late in a long, chronic course.
It is at an early stage

Early disease may show a normal examination and exertional symptoms only. Tell: dyspnea at rest and right heart failure are features of progression and advanced disease, the opposite end of his 9-year course from the early stage.

His chest film shows nodular opacities, 1-10 mm across, throughout both lungs, and eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows organic dust and shows small nodular densities sparing the apices and the bases. Tell: sand is inorganic silica, and eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes belongs to silicosis.

Correct. Sandblasting is a free crystalline silica exposure, and silicosis shows silicotic nodules 1-10 mm across throughout the lungs with eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes. Dyspnea, cough, weight loss, fatigue and crackles fit its presentation.

Sarcoidosis also enlarges the hilar nodes, with symmetric bilateral hilar and right paratracheal adenopathy. Tell: twenty years of sandblasting and eggshell calcification of the nodes point to silica, and his history, not the film alone, names the disease.

Asbestosis follows insulation, demolition, shipyard or construction work and shows pleural plaques with streaking at the bases. Tell: his exposure is silica sand, and eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes is a silicosis sign.

opts: Oxygen is supportive care, as in coal workers' pneumoconiosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tell: progressive pulmonary lesions are an indication for treating the granulomatous disease itself, so supportive oxygen alone leaves the indication untreated.

Correct. Immunosuppressive medications, most commonly methotrexate, azathioprine or infliximab, are used in patients who are intolerant of corticosteroids or have corticosteroid-refractory disease. Her progressive pulmonary lesions still need treatment, and her intolerance moves her to one of these.

She could not tolerate corticosteroids, and intolerance is exactly the setting in which an immunosuppressant is used instead. Tell: methotrexate, azathioprine or infliximab replaces the steroid for patients like her, rather than a second attempt at the same drug.
ruled out by a stated finding

Bronchodilators are supportive treatment in hypersensitivity pneumonitis, beside oxygen and pain medication. Tell: her progressive pulmonary lesions are an indication for disease treatment, and the named steroid alternatives are methotrexate, azathioprine and infliximab.

opts: Progressive fibrosis over several areas, built up over several years, is the chest film of idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia and one of the criteria for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Tell: it supports idiopathic fibrosis rather than moving away from it.
Pleural plaques at the lung bases

Pleural plaques, with linear streaking at the bases, are the most common chest film finding in asbestosis. Tell: plaques point to asbestos exposure, while hilar and mediastinal lymph node enlargement points to sarcoidosis or silicosis.

Correct. Hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy on a chest film points to sarcoidosis or silicosis. Sarcoidosis shows symmetric bilateral hilar and right paratracheal adenopathy, and silicosis can show eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes.
Increased markings in the lower lung fields

Increased interstitial markings in the lower lung fields are the radiograph of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Tell: that finding favors the diagnosis the question asks you to move away from; lymph node enlargement points to sarcoidosis or silicosis.

opts: Antiglomerular and antipulmonary alveolar basement membrane antibodies identify Goodpasture syndrome, with glomerulonephritis and diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage in young adults. Tell: she has no hemorrhage or kidney findings, and the collagen vascular screen is the antinuclear antibody.

An elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level is seen in 40-80% of patients with sarcoidosis. Tell: she has no hilar adenopathy to suggest sarcoidosis, and the test for collagen vascular disease is the antinuclear antibody.

Correct. A high antinuclear antibody points to the collagen vascular diseases, the connective tissue disorders such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome and systemic sclerosis that produce an inflammatory, fibrotic interstitial response. With no exposures or drugs, an autoimmune cause is the next to consider.

A positive cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a granulomatous vasculitis. Tell: the clinician wants a collagen vascular screen, and the test paired with collagen vascular disease is the antinuclear antibody.

opts: Correct. A conservative fluid protocol, targeting a central venous pressure under 4 mm Hg, is preferred, and restrictive fluids significantly increase ventilator-free days and shorten intensive care stays. His hemodynamic stability allows that restrictive approach.
Liberal fluids to support oxygen delivery

Liberal fluids run against the conservative protocol that increases ventilator-free days. Tell: the preferred strategy is restrictive, with a low central venous pressure target, once the patient is hemodynamically stable like him.

Inotrope-driven excessive oxygen delivery causes potential harm, so supranormal targets are avoided. Tell: the preferred hemodynamic strategy is restrictive fluids, not pushing oxygen delivery above normal with drugs.
Fluids guided by a routine pulmonary artery catheter

Routine pulmonary artery catheters offer no clinical benefit in acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: fluids follow a conservative protocol, and cardiac function is assessed with echocardiography rather than a catheter.

opts: Correct. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis produces restrictive dysfunction with a reduced diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide. Simple disease can leave testing unimpressive, but his complicated, symptomatic disease brings the restrictive pattern and impaired gas transfer.

His dust-scarred lungs produce restrictive dysfunction, and the diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide is reduced, not raised. Tell: both halves of this answer run opposite to the expected result in coal workers' pneumoconiosis.

Normal-looking results fit simple disease at most, where pulmonary function testing can be unimpressive. Tell: his complicated disease is restrictive, and the diffusing capacity falls rather than rises as scarring impairs gas transfer.

Restriction is right, but scarring reduces the diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide rather than raising it. Tell: the expected pairing in coal workers' pneumoconiosis is restriction with a low diffusing capacity.

opts: Correct. A ferruginous body is a histologic finding in interstitial lung disease that results from inorganic dust inhalation, and in tissue it suggests significant asbestos exposure. His years in shipyards are a listed asbestos setting, with insulation, demolition and construction.

Sarcoidosis tissue shows noncaseating granulomas, and active disease raises the erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Tell: ferruginous bodies come from inorganic dust inhalation, matching his shipyard asbestos exposure rather than granulomas.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis histology shows interstitial lymphocytes and plasma cells with non-caseating granulomas, from organic dust. Tell: ferruginous bodies come from inorganic dust, the opposite category, as in his shipyard work.

Mesothelioma is diagnosed from pleural fluid cytology in a patient with an effusion. Tell: a ferruginous body marks significant exposure, not cancer; mesothelioma remains a risk, about 10% over a lifetime in asbestos workers.

set2.q: A 35-year-old man with stable sarcoidosis is planning his yearly follow-up. He will have a physical examination, pulmonary function testing, a chest film, an electrocardiogram and a chemistry panel. Which referral completes his yearly evaluation?
opts: Transbronchial lung or fine-needle node biopsy confirms sarcoidosis by showing noncaseating granulomas, a one-time diagnostic step. Tell: yearly follow-up lists an examination, function tests, a film, an electrocardiogram, chemistry and an eye evaluation, not repeat biopsy.

Bronchoalveolar lavage appears among the diagnostic studies for idiopathic interstitial pneumonia and shows milky fluid in silicosis. Tell: it is not part of yearly sarcoidosis follow-up, which instead adds an ophthalmologic evaluation for ocular inflammation.

Lung transplant may be indicated in severe coal workers' pneumoconiosis and is listed among hypersensitivity pneumonitis treatments. Tell: his disease is stable, and the yearly referral every patient with sarcoidosis needs is an eye examination.

Correct. Patients with sarcoidosis require a yearly physical examination, pulmonary function testing, chest film, electrocardiogram, chemistry panel and ophthalmologic evaluation. The eye examination identifies and manages ocular inflammation, which matters because iritis and uveitis are indications for corticosteroids.

She has no exposures, medicines, connective tissue disease or sarcoidosis findings, and computed tomography shows fibrosis that does not settle the subtype of idiopathic interstitial pneumonia. What is the next step?
opts: Lung biopsy to define the subtype

Correct. Idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia may require biopsy for diagnosis, and treatment plan and prognosis depend on the subtype diagnosed. The rule that spares biopsy applies to patients over 65 who meet all four criteria; she is 46 and her scan leaves the subtype open.

Diagnosing idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis without biopsy rests on age over 65 plus all four criteria, including diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing. Tell: she is 46 and her scan does not settle the subtype, so neither condition of that rule is met.

Yearly ophthalmologic evaluation belongs to sarcoidosis follow-up, to identify and manage ocular inflammation. Tell: she has no sarcoidosis findings, and her need is a tissue diagnosis of her idiopathic pneumonia subtype.

Lung transplant is listed for severe coal workers' pneumoconiosis and among hypersensitivity pneumonitis treatments, at the far end of care. Tell: she has no diagnosed subtype yet, and the subtype sets her treatment plan and prognosis.

A conservative fluid protocol, targeting a central venous pressure under 4 mm Hg, increases ventilator-free days. Tell: restrictive fluids are recommended in this syndrome, not avoided, and his stability allows them.
Transfusing at a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL is the recommended threshold, because higher hemoglobin targets do not improve outcomes. Tell: this threshold is part of care, not a practice to avoid.

Sedatives, analgesics and antipyretics reduce oxygen demand in acute respiratory distress syndrome and are used appropriately. Tell: they are part of care, while the routine catheter is what offers no clinical benefit.

set2.q: A 72-year-old man with no occupational, drug or connective tissue disease history has 2 years of insidious dry cough and exertional dyspnea. He has bibasilar inspiratory crackles, pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern, chest films over several years show progressive fibrosis, and high-resolution computed tomography shows diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing. How should the diagnosis be established?
opts: Correct. Over age 65, idiopathic disease with inspiratory crackles, restrictive physiology, radiographic progressive fibrosis over several years and diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing on high-resolution computed tomography give idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with 90% confidence. Such patients do not need surgical lung biopsy.

Idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia may require biopsy when the picture is incomplete. Tell: he is over 65 and meets all four criteria, which is the situation in which surgical lung biopsy is not needed for the diagnosis.

Antibodies to an inhaled agent in serum give the definitive diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, after an organic dust exposure. Tell: he has no exposures, and his findings are the four criteria for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis instead.

Transbronchial lung biopsy or fine-needle node biopsy showing noncaseating granulomas confirms sarcoidosis. Tell: he has no hilar adenopathy or multi-organ findings; his age and honeycombing fit idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, which needs no biopsy here.

opts: Bronchodilators are among the supportive treatments for hypersensitivity pneumonitis, with oxygen and pain medication. Tell: supportive therapy is used, not avoided; the thing to avoid is the agent itself, the moldy hay.

Oxygen is a listed supportive treatment for hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which can cause hypoxia. Tell: it is used when needed; the moldy hay that caused his farmer's lung is what he must avoid on his return.

Pain medication appears with oxygen and bronchodilators as supportive treatment for hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tell: none of the supportive therapies is the problem; renewed contact with moldy hay is.

Correct. Treatment of hypersensitivity pneumonitis is to identify the responsible agent and avoid it, and moldy hay is the source of farmer's lung. Continued exposure may lead to a worsened disease state, while symptoms caught early can be reversible.

set2.q: A 55-year-old woman is leaving the hospital after acute respiratory distress syndrome from pneumonia. She asks how long her lung function will take to recover. Which answer is accurate?
opts: One month is too soon: pulmonary function improves over 6 to 12 months after this syndrome. Tell: recovery is measured in most of a year, not weeks, and some functional deficits often remain even then.
Three months falls short of the usual course, which runs 6 to 12 months. Tell: she should expect lung function to keep improving well beyond 3 months, while some deficits may persist.

Correct. Lung function generally recovers over 6 to 12 months after acute respiratory distress syndrome, though functional deficits often remain, with residual diffusion deficits persisting. Physical sequelae after intensive care, such as muscle wasting, weakness and fatigue, also need attention.

Three years overshoots the typical recovery window of 6 to 12 months after acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: lasting deficits can remain, but the main recovery of lung function happens within about a year.

set2.q: A 63-year-old woman with interstitial lung disease has a computed tomography scan showing established fibrosis with honeycombing. She asks whether the scarring will heal once the inflammation settles. Which response is accurate?
opts: Settling inflammation does not undo scar: the collagen laid down after alveolitis is permanent scar tissue that leaves the lung stiff. Tell: reversibility belongs to early disease caught before scarring, as in hypersensitivity pneumonitis treated promptly, not to established honeycombing.

Corticosteroids appear in the plans for sarcoidosis and severe hypersensitivity pneumonitis, aimed at active inflammation. Tell: the scar itself is permanent tissue, and honeycombing marks late disease, so no medicine is described as dissolving it.

Breathing exercises do not reshape scar: fibrosis permanently damages the alveoli and leaves the lung stiff and restrictive. Tell: rehabilitation appears among supportive measures in pneumoconiosis, which ease symptoms rather than remove scar tissue.

Correct. Fibrosis is the lung's response to an inflammatory source: alveolitis drives fibroblasts to lay down collagen, forming permanent scar tissue that damages the alveoli, stiffens the lung and impairs gas exchange. Honeycombing is a late finding, so her scarring is established and will not heal.

set2.q: A 52-year-old man has acute bird fancier's lung from the pigeons he keeps at home, and his symptoms are settling. He asks whether he can keep the birds if he takes medicine whenever symptoms flare. Which counsel is accurate?
opts: Continued exposure may worsen his disease

Correct. Prompt diagnosis is key so the patient can be removed from the irritating environment: symptoms can be reversible if caught early, but continued exposure may lead to a worsened disease state. Treatment starts with identifying and avoiding the agent, here his birds.

Corticosteroids may help severe cases, but treatment starts with avoiding the agent. Tell: no medicine is described as making continued exposure safe, and continued exposure may worsen the disease toward its chronic form.
His lung damage is already permanent

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis symptoms can be reversible if caught early, and acute disease shows little change on imaging. Tell: his acute illness is settling, so his outcome still depends on removing the birds now.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a non-atopic, non-asthmatic inflammatory disease from inhaled organic dust. Tell: his reaction is to the bird antigen itself, so treating it as asthma leaves the exposure in place.

set2.q: A 30-year-old man has started work in building demolition, where he handles old asbestos insulation. He asks how long after exposure asbestos lung disease usually leads people to seek care. Which answer is accurate?
opts: Asbestos disease does not usually surface within a year; the course runs 10-20 years, with care sought at about 15. Tell: illness within hours of each exposure fits hypersensitivity pneumonitis from organic dust, not asbestos.

Five years is well short of the usual course: patients usually seek medical attention about 15 years after asbestos exposure. Tell: the timeline to remember is 10-20 years, centered on 15, so 5 years is too early.

Correct. Asbestosis develops over 10-20 years, and patients usually seek medical attention about 15 years after exposure. That long delay is why an exposure history matters in an older patient with dyspnea, and why a young worker's risk starts with exposure he has now.
Forty years overshoots the usual interval of about 15 years from asbestos exposure to seeking care. Tell: the stated course of asbestosis is 10-20 years, so 40 years lies far outside it.

set2.q: A 57-year-old woman with acute respiratory distress syndrome from sepsis has a hemoglobin of 8.2 g/dL (normal 12.0-15.5) and no active bleeding. Her family asks that she be transfused to bring the value back to normal. Which should be avoided?
opts: Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: it is a step to take when severity allows, not one to avoid, and it has nothing to do with her hemoglobin.
Transfusing if it falls to 7 g/dL

A hemoglobin of 7 g/dL is the threshold at which to transfuse in this syndrome. Tell: transfusing at that level is recommended; it is transfusing up to normal that higher-target evidence fails to support.

Correct. In acute respiratory distress syndrome the transfusion threshold is a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL, and higher hemoglobin targets do not improve patient outcomes. Her 8.2 g/dL is low against the 12.0-15.5 range but above the threshold, so transfusing toward normal offers no outcome benefit.

A conservative fluid protocol increases ventilator-free days and shortens intensive care stays. Tell: it is recommended care in this syndrome, unlike chasing a normal hemoglobin with transfusion, which brings no outcome benefit.

set2.q: A 32-year-old woman newly diagnosed with sarcoidosis asks what caused her lung disease. Which response is accurate?
opts: Medicines such as methotrexate, amiodarone and nitrofurantoin cause treatment-related interstitial disease, a group of known cause. Tell: sarcoidosis is classed with the interstitial lung diseases of unknown etiology, not with drug causes.

Correct. Sarcoidosis is a multi-organ disease of idiopathic cause, one of the interstitial lung diseases of unknown etiology with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. It is thought to arise from environmental triggers, such as infections, inhaled agents or mold, in a genetically predisposed person, but its etiology remains unknown.

Asbestos fibers cause asbestosis and mesothelioma, interstitial disease of known occupational cause after insulation, demolition, shipyard or construction work. Tell: she has no such exposure, and sarcoidosis sits in the unknown-cause group.

Genetic predisposition is part of the proposed picture, but it acts together with environmental triggers, and the etiology is listed as unknown. Tell: no single inherited cause is named for sarcoidosis, only a predisposed person meeting a trigger.
